clue.text: "She stole along, she nothing spoke, / The sighs she heaved were soft and low"

definitions.text: "She stole along, she nothing spoke, / The sighs she heaved were soft and low"

parts.words: "She stole along, she nothing spoke, / The sighs she heaved were soft and low"
parts.note: these lines come from Coleridge's unfinished Gothic poem, and the solver names the heroine they describe, who steals through the castle at night

explanation.surface: A quoted couplet about a woman creeping silently through the dark, sighing softly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is a quotation; the answer is the title and heroine of the Coleridge poem it comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: The lines describe the lady of Coleridge's poem as she slips into the woods at midnight, so the quotation identifies that poem's title character.

clue.text: Harem I turned inside out to find Dream girl

indicators.note: turned inside out says the letters of these two words are thoroughly rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone ransacks a harem in search of the girl of their dreams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dream girl' sounds like an ideal woman, but 'Dream' is Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, whose young lovers include this Athenian girl.
explanation.definitionFit: She is one of the two young women lost in the wood in Shakespeare's comedy, so a girl from the 'Dream'.

clue.text: Hopkins apparently saw the animating energy of art in emphasis

definitions.text: Hopkins apparently saw the animating energy of art

parts.note: taken as written
emphasis on a syllable or point is stress

explanation.surface: A remark that Gerard Manley Hopkins found the life force of art lay in emphasis.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has no letter count. Gerard Manley Hopkins coined this word, alongside 'inscape', for the force that holds a thing's inner form and strikes the beholder.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the poet-priest's own coinage for the energy that sustains a thing's distinctive form and conveys it to the mind, his theory of artistic vitality.

clue.text: Behan's long time following the army

indicators.note: following places the long time after the words naming the army

parts.note: taken as written
a host is an archaic word for an army
an age is a very long time

explanation.surface: A long stint of service following the army, as a soldier's memoir might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: Brendan Behan was an Irish playwright; the possessive 'Behan's' stands for a work of his, the 1958 play about an English soldier held by the IRA in a Dublin lodging house.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of Brendan Behan's best-known play after The Quare Fellow, so 'Behan's' points to it.

clue.text: Canon for poet,

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held is 'Canon for poet, (7)': it ends on a comma and is cut short, so the wordplay for BROCARD is missing; no scan or reprint gives the rest.

clue.text: Taylor's Pastoral

parts.note: Bayard Taylor, the American poet, wrote a long narrative poem subtitled 'A Pastoral of Norway', and the clue wants its title

explanation.surface: A bare reference to a pastoral poem by a writer named Taylor.
explanation.walkthrough: Bayard Taylor's 1873 poem is titled after its Norwegian hero, with the subtitle 'A Pastoral of Norway'.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the Norwegian poem by the American writer Bayard Taylor is the hero's first name, so it is 'Taylor's Pastoral'.

clue.text: French pacifist to forbid kiss at first encounter

parts.note: to bar something is to forbid it
buss is an old word for a kiss

indicators.note: at first asks for only the opening letter of the word encounter

explanation.surface: A French peace campaigner refuses any kissing when meeting someone for the first time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first encounter' reads as a time phrase but gives only the E of 'encounter'. Henri Barbusse wrote the anti-war novel Le Feu.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Barbusse was a French novelist whose war book Under Fire made him a leading campaigner against war.

clue.text: Some good men conceal name of literary critic

parts.note: saints are holy, virtuous people, so some good men
to bury something is to hide it away

explanation.surface: A few virtuous men cover up the name of a critic.
explanation.walkthrough: George Saintsbury was a prolific English literary critic and historian of literature.
explanation.definitionFit: George Saintsbury was an English scholar and reviewer famous for his histories of literature and prosody.

clue.text: An artist holds tin for secrets

parts.note: the article an gives the single letter

indicators.note: holds says the word for an artist encloses the word for tin

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist
a tin is a can

explanation.surface: A painter keeps a tin box full of secrets.
explanation.definitionFit: Arcana are hidden mysteries or specialist knowledge known only to initiates.

clue.text: Duke of Milan may do well with ring

parts.note: to prosper is to thrive or do well
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: An Italian duke could thrive if he married, or wore a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The rightful Duke of Milan is the magician of Shakespeare's The Tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Tempest the exiled magician on the island is the deposed ruler of the Italian city.

clue.text: Eco's publisher's reader encountered in Miss Evans's provincial town?

definitions.meaning: in Umberto Eco's novel Foucault's Pendulum the narrator works as a reader for the publisher Garamond

definitions.text: encountered in Miss Evans's provincial town?
definitions.meaning: Miss Evans is George Eliot, whose novel about a provincial town includes the dry scholar whom Dorothea marries

explanation.surface: A publisher's reader for Eco is met in a provincial town described by a lady writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Ann Evans wrote as George Eliot; her 'provincial town' is Middlemarch, subtitled 'A Study of Provincial Life'. The question mark marks that allusive second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname is shared by Eco's narrator, who reads manuscripts for a Milan publisher, and the pedantic clergyman scholar of Middlemarch.

clue.text: Rich Windsor gentleman turned by reader

definitions.meaning: in The Merry Wives of Windsor Master and Mistress ... are a well-off citizen couple
a book's leaves are turned over one by one as someone reads

explanation.surface: A wealthy gentleman from Windsor is won round by someone reading to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Master Page is the well-to-do burgher of Shakespeare's Windsor comedy, and a leaf of a book is what a reader turns.

clue.text: Raskolnikov's was admittedly due

parts.note: Raskolnikov is the murderer of Dostoevsky's novel, so after his confessed crime the second half of the title was owed to him

explanation.surface: A comment that Dostoevsky's student murderer had something coming to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admittedly' points to Raskolnikov's confession; Dostoevsky's novel is Crime and ... , and what follows the crime is what he was due.
explanation.definitionFit: Raskolnikov confesses to murder and is sentenced to Siberia, the penalty completing the title Crime and ...

clue.text: Twelve-tone music does, in common with the publishers of Dickens

definitions.text: Twelve-tone music does, in common with the publishers of Dickens

parts.words: Twelve-tone music does, in common with the publishers of Dickens
parts.note: twelve-tone composition arranges a note row in a fixed series, and Dickens's publishers issued his novels in monthly instalments

explanation.surface: A note that Schoenberg's music and Victorian publishers share a habit.
explanation.walkthrough: Twelve-tone (serial) music orders pitches in a series; Dickens's novels first appeared in parts. The verb covers both.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to arrange in a series, as twelve-tone composers do with notes, and to publish in instalments, as Dickens's novels were.

clue.text: It may be placed on a pedestal by one preparing his column

definitions.text: It may be placed on a pedestal by one preparing his column

parts.words: It may be placed on a pedestal by one preparing his column
parts.note: the column is an architectural one, and its builder may set an ornament on a plinth at the peak or corners of the pediment

explanation.surface: A newspaper columnist sets something up on a pedestal to admire it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'column' suggests journalism, but it is an architectural column; the answer is the ornament or statue set on a small pedestal on a classical building.
explanation.definitionFit: In classical architecture this is a plinth-mounted ornament set at the apex or corners of a pediment above the columns.

clue.text: Reporter offering points on island

parts.note: the compass points north, east, west and south give N, E, W and S
the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A journalist making points while stationed on an island.
explanation.definitionFit: A journalist who gathers and reports stories is a reporter.

clue.text: He had his chips at Brookfield

definitions.text: He had his chips at Brookfield

parts.words: He had his chips at Brookfield
parts.note: Brookfield is the school in James Hilton's Goodbye, Mr Chips, and its headmaster hired the young teacher nicknamed Chips

explanation.surface: Someone who failed, or ate a fried supper, at a place called Brookfield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'had his chips' suggests failure or a meal; it means the Brookfield headmaster who took on Mr Chipping, nicknamed Chips, in Hilton's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: In Goodbye, Mr Chips the headmaster at Brookfield School is the man who appoints the young Mr Chipping.

clue.text: German woman takes direction for American poet

indicators.note: takes means the word for a German woman receives the direction inside it

parts.note: Frau is German for a married woman
ENE is east-north-east, a compass direction

explanation.surface: A German lady picks a direction to follow an American poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Philip Freneau was the 'poet of the American Revolution'.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Freneau was an eighteenth-century writer of verse from New York, called the poet of the American Revolution.

clue.text: Quite unlike the philosophy of August Comte

definitions.text: Quite unlike the philosophy of August Comte

parts.words: Quite unlike the philosophy of August Comte
parts.note: Comte founded positivism, and the clue wants the word for its opposite

explanation.surface: A comparison of something with the ideas of the French philosopher Comte.
explanation.walkthrough: Auguste Comte founded positivism, so something 'quite unlike' his philosophy is its opposite: not positive.
explanation.definitionFit: The opposite of positive is its contrary, so a stance quite unlike Comte's positivism.

clue.text: Joint author of Westward Ho!, we hear

definitions.text: Joint author of Westward Ho!, we hear

parts.words: Joint author of Westward Ho!, we hear
parts.note: the Jacobean comedy Westward Ho was written by Thomas Dekker with a collaborator, also the surname of a famous American dictionary-maker

explanation.surface: Gossip about who co-wrote a play called Westward Ho!
explanation.walkthrough: Westward Ho! here is the 1604 city comedy by Dekker and John Webster, not Kingsley's novel; 'we hear' points to Webster's dictionary, the authority on how words are spoken and spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: John Webster wrote the comedy with Thomas Dekker, and the surname is also that of the American lexicographer whose dictionary records words.

clue.text: The payment for Russell Haley's pioneering, postmodernist novel?

definitions.meaning: a payment made to clear a debt or claim
the New Zealand writer Russell Haley published a novel of that title, and the word also means a colony founded by pioneers

explanation.surface: A remark on the fee paid for a pioneering postmodern novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pioneering' hints at the other sense, a colonial community set up by pioneers, as well as the novel's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A final payment in a dispute is a settling of accounts, and Haley's novel took that word, which also means a pioneers' colony, as its title.

clue.text: Poet makes us beam (with gravity)

parts.note: g is the symbol for acceleration due to gravity
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: A poet causes us to smile, though solemnly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beam' reads as smile and 'gravity' as solemnity, but they are a ray and the physics symbol g. Thomas Gray wrote the Elegy in a Country Churchyard.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gray was the eighteenth-century English author of the Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.

clue.text: One of David's mighty men and "as light of foot as a wild roe" (Samuel)

definitions.text: One of David's mighty men and "as light of foot as a wild roe" (Samuel)

parts.words: One of David's mighty men and "as light of foot as a wild roe" (Samuel)
parts.note: the Second Book of Samuel describes Joab's brother, one of David's warriors, as swift of foot like a wild roe

explanation.surface: A biblical description of one of King David's fleet-footed warriors.
explanation.walkthrough: 2 Samuel 2:18 says this brother of Joab was 'as light of foot as a wild roe'; he was killed by Abner.
explanation.definitionFit: Joab's brother is listed among David's thirty mighty men and is described in Samuel as swift as a wild roe.

clue.text: Wrongly name case for Roman arts patron

indicators.note: wrongly signals that these two words are put together in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone misnames the case of an ancient Roman benefactor.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaius Maecenas backed Virgil and Horace, and his name became a byword for a patron.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaius Maecenas was the wealthy adviser to Augustus who supported Virgil and Horace, the model of a sponsor of the arts.

clue.text: Small rise and fall quoted in one appropriate work

indicators.note: quoted in says the letters are sitting within the words one appropriate

explanation.surface: A minor rise and fall is cited in a suitable piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a tide with the least difference between high and low water.
explanation.definitionFit: A neap tide, around the moon's quarters, has the smallest range between high and low water.

clue.text: Edith Wharton's repose

parts.note: Edith Wharton wrote a 1927 novel whose title pairs a word for dusk with sleep, so her repose is that kind of sleep

explanation.surface: A mention of the American novelist Edith Wharton taking a rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Wharton's novel is Twilight Sleep (1927); 'repose' stands for sleep, and the answer is the word before it in the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Wharton's novel takes its title from a drug-induced semi-conscious state used in childbirth, the first word of which is the answer.

clue.text: The world of existence to him seemed to have lazily melted dxwn into a mere

definitions.text: The world of existence to him seemed to have lazily melted dxwn into a mere

parts.words: The world of existence to him seemed to have lazily melted dxwn into a mere
parts.note: a quotation with its last word left out, a misty cloud of matter, which the solver supplies

explanation.surface: A quoted sentence about a man for whom the whole world has dissolved into vagueness.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing last word is a hazy cloud. 'dxwn' is an OCR slip for 'down'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloud of gas and dust in space is a byword for vague, formless haze, what the world melts into in the sentence.

clue.text: Nobel Prize-winning author of Henry IV

definitions.text: Nobel Prize-winning author of Henry IV

parts.words: Nobel Prize-winning author of Henry IV
parts.note: Henry IV here is not Shakespeare's history but the 1922 Italian play about a man who believes he is the German emperor

explanation.surface: A question about which Nobel laureate wrote a play called Henry IV.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare never won a Nobel; the Henry IV meant is Enrico IV (1922) by the Italian dramatist who won the 1934 Nobel Prize.
explanation.definitionFit: Luigi Pirandello, Italian dramatist and 1934 Nobel laureate, wrote Enrico IV, known in English as Henry IV.
